title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 22: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: Sauce for the Poor Goose and the Rich Gander
keywords: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals
sufficient importance to merit its attention
primary_topics: Chapter 22 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's dissent from the Court en banc's 8-7 decision to take over Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals from the Third Division, which he argued was done without any cogent or compelling reason.

An explanatory account of how the Supreme Court is organized into the Banc and three Divisions, how cases are raffled and referred, and why a Division's decision is a coequal judgment of the Court rather than one subject to appeal to the full Court.

His charge of a double standard: the same Banc had refused to take over the Sumilao farmers' case in Fortich v. Corona despite a genuine 2-2 deadlock, yet took over this 99-hectare land case for not-so-poor private petitioners on the bare invocation of 'sufficient importance.'

The postscript that the 8-7 Resolution contravened the unanimous en banc Resolution in AM No. 99-8-06-SC, which provided that motions for reconsideration in Division cases shall be acted upon by the Division itself.
sub_topics: The constitutional design: Article VIII, Section 4 lets the Court sit en banc or in divisions, and the present Court sits en banc and in three Divisions of five, with the Chief Justice presiding over the Banc and one Division and the two most senior justices chairing the others.

The Banc and the Divisions deliberate independently and their decisions are coequal judgments, so that 'some people say that there are really four Supreme Courts,' subject only to the caveat that a doctrine may be modified or reversed solely by the Court en banc.
The workload picture: Annual Report statistics show that about 85 to 90 percent of decisions come from the Divisions and only 10 to 15 percent from the Banc.

How cases reach the Banc: the enumerated en banc cases under Article VIII, Section 4(2), the Raffle Committee's preliminary determination, and the nine categories of Circular 2-89 as amended by the full Court Resolution of November 18, 1993 -- including Item 8, under which three members of a Division may seek referral.

The facts of the takeover: the consolidated Firestone and Republic cases were decided unanimously by the Third Division on September 2, 1999 in a ponencia by Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes; the Division then rejected a motion to refer them to the full Court 4-1, with Justice Purisima the lone negative vote.

At Justice Purisima's instance, the Banc on June 28, 2000 nevertheless 'yanked' the cases out of and against the will of the Division, invoking paragraph 9 of Circular 2-89, the 99-hectare area of the land and the cases' 'sufficient importance.'

The 8-7 line-up: Chief Justice Davide and Justices Bellosillo, Kapunan, Mendoza, Purisima, Buena, Santiago and De Leon for the takeover; Justices Melo, Puno, Vitug, Panganiban, Quisumbing, Pardo and Reyes against.

Justice Reyes's main Dissent: the size of the property is nowhere a ground for referral, the validity of OCT No. 4216 was long settled in three final judgments, the pending Motion for Reconsideration belonged to the Division that rendered the Decision, the Banc is not an appellate court, the November 18, 1993 Resolution was essentially an amendment to Rule 136 on the form of papers, and the Banc should be shielded from aggrieved litigants' importunings.
Justice Puno's one-page dissent urging the Banc to defer while the Third Division intended to hear the Republic's Motion for Reconsideration.

CJP's own dissent: the majority Resolution 'simply pontificates' about sufficient importance without stating why, and the 'lame excuse' about the land's unstated classification is an argument for granting reconsideration, not for a takeover.

The Sumilao comparison that 'specially disturbed and saddened' him: there, a 2-2 vote on reconsideration gave Justice Melo a genuine question of sufficient importance, yet the full Court turned his proposal down with only Justice Vitug and CJP supporting it.

His conclusion demanding consistency -- if the Banc takes this case it should also take the farmers' petition, and having rejected theirs it should reject this one -- because 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander.'
The postscript noting the conflict with AM No. 99-8-06-SC of February 15, 2000, and citing former Justice Isagani A. Cruz's column 'Another Dubious Decision.'

notable_anecdotes: CJP describes the Banc as having 'yanked' the consolidated cases out of and against the will of the Third Division, which had rejected referral 4-1 with Justice Purisima the lone dissenter.
He quotes his own 'anguish' at what he believed was a double standard of justice tilted against the poor.
He recalls that when Justice Melo asked the Banc to resolve the Sumilao farmers' 2-2 deadlock, only he and Justice Vitug supported the proposal.
He closes his dissent with the proverb that sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander -- 'simple, equal justice for all.'

In a postscript he notes that the 8-7 Resolution contradicted a unanimous en banc Resolution promulgated only months earlier, and cites Justice Isagani A. Cruz's newspaper column calling it 'Another Dubious Decision.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' explains how the Supreme Court divides its work and then recounts CJP's dissent from an 8-7 en banc takeover of a case already decided by a Division. He first sets out the structure: Article VIII, Section 4 permits the Court to sit en banc or in divisions, and the Court then sat as a Banc of fifteen and three Divisions of five, whose judgments are coequal, so that some people say there are really four Supreme Courts. About 85 to 90 percent of decisions come from the Divisions. Referral to the Banc is governed by the constitutional enumeration and by Circular 2-89 as amended in 1993, whose Item 8 allows three members of a Division to seek referral. In Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals and its companion Republic case, the Third Division unanimously ruled for private respondents on September 2, 1999 in a ponencia by Justice Gonzaga-Reyes and then refused referral 4-1, with Justice Purisima alone dissenting. At his instance the Banc, on June 28, 2000, took the cases over anyway, invoking paragraph 9 of the Circular, the land's 99-hectare size and the cases' sufficient importance. Justice Reyes dissented on five grounds, including that the Banc is not an appellate court and that the pending Motion for Reconsideration belonged to her Division; Justice Puno urged deferral. CJP argued that the majority gave no cogent or compelling reason and merely pontificated. What disturbed him most was the contrast with the Sumilao farmers' case, where a genuine 2-2 deadlock had not persuaded the Banc to intervene, with only he and Justice Vitug supporting Justice Melo's proposal. He demanded consistency: take both cases or neither, for sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander. A postscript notes that the Resolution contravened the unanimous AM No. 99-8-06-SC of February 15, 2000, which assigned motions for reconsideration to the deciding Division.
